notes.front: What 1947 incident is popularly tied to the word "bug" in computing?
notes.back: Operators of the Harvard Mark II (Grace Hopper's team) taped a moth found in a relay into the logbook as the "first actual case of bug being found". The term "bug" for engineering faults predates this (Edison used it in the 1870s).

notes.front: Who is credited (1957) with first distinguishing testing from debugging?
notes.back: Charles L. Baker, in a review of Dan McCracken's book Digital Computer Programming: debugging = making the program run; testing = making sure it solves the problem.

notes.front: Gelperin & Hetzel (1988) divided testing history into five eras. Name them.
notes.back:
• Debugging-oriented (to 1956)
  • Demonstration-oriented (1957–1978): show it works
  • Destruction-oriented (1979–1982): find errors
  • Evaluation-oriented (1983–1987): quality across the lifecycle
  • Prevention-oriented (1988–): prevent defects
notes.source: Gelperin & Hetzel, "The Growth of Software Testing", Communications of the ACM, 1988

notes.front: Edsger Dijkstra's famous limit on testing (circa 1969–1970)?
notes.back: "Program testing can be used to show the presence of bugs, but never to show their absence!" — motivation for formal methods and for humility about green test suites.
notes.source: Dijkstra, Notes on Structured Programming / NATO Software Engineering conference 1969

notes.front: What book and definition marked the "destruction-oriented" era (1979)?
notes.back: Glenford Myers, The Art of Software Testing: testing is the process of executing a program with the intent of finding errors. A successful test is one that finds a bug.

notes.front: What is the significance of the 1972 Chapel Hill symposium?
notes.back: Organized by Bill Hetzel at the University of North Carolina, it is generally considered the first conference devoted to software testing ("Computer Program Test Methods").

notes.front: Who introduced mutation testing and with which two hypotheses?
notes.back:
Richard Lipton proposed it (~1971); DeMillo, Lipton & Sayward formalized it in 1978. Hypotheses:
  • Competent programmer: real programs are close to correct, so faults are small syntactic deviations.
  • Coupling effect: tests that catch simple faults also catch most complex ones.
notes.source: DeMillo, Lipton, Sayward, "Hints on Test Data Selection", 1978

notes.front: What did Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) 829 (1983) standardize, and what replaced it?
notes.back: Software test documentation (test plan, design, case, procedure, incident, summary reports). Superseded by International Organization for Standardization (ISO)/IEC/IEEE 29119 (from 2013).

notes.front: Where did fuzzing originate?
notes.back: Barton Miller's 1988 University of Wisconsin class project: feed random input to UNIX utilities. The 1990 paper found roughly a quarter to a third of utilities crashed or hung. Modern coverage-guided fuzzing: American Fuzzy Lop (AFL) by Michał Zalewski (2013), libFuzzer.

notes.front: Who created SUnit and JUnit, and when?
notes.back: Kent Beck wrote SUnit for Smalltalk (~1994). Kent Beck and Erich Gamma wrote JUnit (1997, reportedly on a flight to the Object-Oriented Programming, Systems, Languages & Applications (OOPSLA) conference). This spawned the "xUnit" family.

notes.front: When was Test-Driven Development (TDD) popularized and by whom?
notes.back: Kent Beck, via Extreme Programming (XP) (late 1990s) and the book Test-Driven Development: By Example (2002). Beck describes it as a rediscovery of older test-first practice.

notes.front: Who coined Behaviour-Driven Development (BDD), and why?
notes.back: Dan North (article "Introducing BDD", 2006; JBehave from ~2003). Teaching TDD, he found people stuck on "test" vocabulary (what to test, where to start, what to call it). Replacing "test" with "behaviour"/"should" sentences fixed that.

notes.front: Origin of Cucumber and Gherkin?
notes.back: Aslak Hellesøy created Cucumber (Ruby, 2008), growing out of the RSpec Story Runner. Gherkin is its plain-language Given/When/Then syntax, now used by SpecFlow/Reqnroll, Behave, JBehave and others.

notes.front: Where does QuickCheck / property-based testing come from?
notes.back: Koen Claessen and John Hughes, QuickCheck for Haskell (International Conference on Functional Programming (ICFP), 2000). Descendants: Hypothesis (Python), fast-check (JavaScript), jqwik (Java), proptest (Rust).

notes.front: Who introduced the Test Pyramid and what does it say?
notes.back: Mike Cohn, Succeeding with Agile (2009): many fast unit tests at the base, fewer service/integration tests, very few User Interface (UI)/End-to-End (E2E) tests at the top. Inverted version = "ice-cream cone" anti-pattern.

notes.front: What is the Testing Trophy?
notes.back: Kent C. Dodds (2018): static analysis at the base, a thin unit layer, a large integration layer, small E2E (End-to-End) top. Argument: integration tests give the best confidence per cost for typical web apps.

notes.front: Who created the Agile Testing Quadrants?
notes.back: Brian Marick (2003); popularized by Lisa Crispin & Janet Gregory, Agile Testing (2009).

notes.front: Who coined "exploratory testing"?
notes.back: Cem Kaner (1980s), later developed by James Bach and others: simultaneous learning, test design and execution, guided by charters and time-boxed sessions (session-based test management).

notes.front: What is chaos engineering and where did it start?
notes.back: Deliberately injecting failures into production-like systems to verify resilience. Netflix's Chaos Monkey (~2010–2011, open-sourced 2012) randomly terminated instances; later the "Simian Army" and Principles of Chaos Engineering.

notes.front: Who coined "test double" and its five kinds?
notes.back: Gerard Meszaros, xUnit Test Patterns (2007): Dummy, Stub, Spy, Mock, Fake.

notes.front: Who popularized "characterization tests" and why do they matter now?
notes.back: Michael Feathers, Working Effectively with Legacy Code (2004): tests that pin down what code currently does before changing it. Directly useful before letting a coding agent refactor legacy code.

notes.front: What is "shift-left" testing and who coined it?
notes.back: Larry Smith (2001): move testing earlier in the lifecycle (requirements, design, Continuous Integration (CI)). Complement: "shift-right" = testing/observing in production (canaries, feature flags, chaos).

notes.front: Verification vs. validation (Barry Boehm)?
notes.back: Verification: are we building the product right (conforms to spec)? Validation: are we building the right product (meets user needs)?

notes.front: Error vs. fault (defect) vs. failure?
notes.back: Error = human mistake. Fault/defect/bug = the resulting flaw in code. Failure = observable incorrect behaviour when the fault is executed. Not every fault causes a failure.

notes.front: What is the test oracle problem?
notes.back: Deciding what the correct output is. Without an oracle a test can only check "didn't crash". Mitigations: properties/invariants, differential testing against a reference, metamorphic relations, golden files, human review.

notes.front: The seven testing principles of the International Software Testing Qualifications Board (ISTQB)?
notes.back:
• Testing shows presence, not absence, of defects
  • Exhaustive testing is impossible
  • Early testing saves time and money
  • Defects cluster together
  • Tests wear out (pesticide paradox)
  • Testing is context dependent
  • Absence-of-defects fallacy

notes.front: What is the pesticide paradox?
notes.back: Boris Beizer: repeating the same tests eventually stops finding new bugs, as bugs adapt to the "pesticide". Suites must be reviewed and new tests/techniques added (property-based, fuzzing, exploratory).

notes.front: What does the absence-of-defects fallacy warn about?
notes.back: A system with no known bugs can still be useless if it doesn't meet user needs. Validation matters as much as verification.

notes.front: What are the FIRST properties of good unit tests?
notes.back: Fast, Independent (Isolated), Repeatable, Self-validating (pass/fail with no human interpretation), Timely (written just before/with the code).

notes.front: What is Arrange-Act-Assert (AAA) and how does it relate to Gherkin?
notes.back: Test structure: set up state (Arrange), perform one action (Act), check outcome (Assert). Gherkin's Given/When/Then maps onto it 1:1.

notes.front: Why test behaviour rather than implementation?
notes.back: Tests coupled to internals (private methods, call order, exact mock interactions) break on harmless refactors and give false failures. Test through public interfaces and observable outcomes so refactoring stays cheap.

notes.front: Coverage types from weakest to strongest?
notes.back: Statement/line → branch/decision → condition → Modified Condition/Decision Coverage (MC/DC; required for the highest level of avionics software under DO-178B/C) → path coverage (usually infeasible).

notes.front: Why is code coverage a poor target?
notes.back: It proves a line ran, not that anything was asserted about it (Goodhart's law). Use it to find untested code, not to certify tested code. Mutation score is the stronger signal.

notes.front: What is a flaky test and common causes?
notes.back: A test that passes and fails without code changes. Causes: timing/sleeps, test order dependence, shared state, network, randomness without seeds, time zones/clock, concurrency, resource leaks. Quarantine and fix; flakiness destroys trust in the suite.

notes.front: What is a hermetic test?
notes.back: A test with all dependencies contained and controlled (no real network, shared databases, or wall-clock time), so results depend only on the code under test. Core to Google's testing approach.

notes.front: Google's test sizes?
notes.back: Small: single process, no I/O beyond memory, no sleeps. Medium: single machine, localhost network allowed. Large: multiple machines/real systems. Size is about resource constraints, not scope.

notes.front: What is the "Beyoncé Rule"?
notes.back: "If you liked it, you should have put a test on it." If a change by infrastructure/other teams breaks your untested behaviour, that's on you.

notes.front: Dummy vs. stub vs. spy vs. mock vs. fake?
notes.back:
• Dummy: passed but never used
  • Stub: returns canned answers
  • Spy: stub that records calls
  • Mock: pre-programmed with expectations, verifies interactions
  • Fake: working lightweight implementation (in-memory database)

notes.front: Why "don't mock what you don't own"?
notes.back: Mocks of third-party APIs encode your assumptions about them, which may be wrong or drift. Wrap the dependency in your own adapter; mock the adapter; test the adapter against the real thing (integration/contract test).
notes.source: Freeman & Pryce, Growing Object-Oriented Software, Guided by Tests

notes.front: Classicist (Detroit) vs. mockist (London) TDD (Test-Driven Development)?
notes.back: Classicist: use real collaborators where cheap, verify state. Mockist: outside-in, mock collaborators, verify interactions. Mockist designs interfaces early but couples tests to implementation more.

notes.front: The TDD (Test-Driven Development) cycle?
notes.back: Red: write a small failing test. Green: simplest code to pass. Refactor: clean up with tests green. Repeat in small steps.

notes.front: Why must you see a new test fail first?
notes.back: A test that passes before the implementation exists may not exercise the new code at all (wrong target, missing assertion, always-true condition). Red proves the test can detect absence of the behaviour.

notes.front: What is approval / snapshot / golden-master testing?
notes.back: Capture output once, have a human approve it, then diff future output against it. Great for complex outputs and legacy code; risk: people blindly re-approve diffs.

notes.front: Black-box vs. white-box vs. grey-box testing?
notes.back: Black-box: designed from specification, no knowledge of internals. White-box: designed from code structure (branches, paths). Grey-box: partial knowledge (e.g. knows the database schema or architecture).

notes.front: Static vs. dynamic testing?
notes.back: Static: examining without executing (reviews, linting, type checking, Static Application Security Testing (SAST)). Dynamic: executing the code.

notes.front: Functional vs. non-functional testing?
notes.back: Functional: does it do the right thing (features, business rules). Non-functional: how well (performance, security, usability, reliability, accessibility, compatibility).

notes.front: Unit test?
notes.back: Tests a small unit (function/class/module) in isolation, fast and deterministic. Definition of "unit" varies: classicists often mean a unit of behaviour, not a single class.

notes.front: Integration test?
notes.back: Verifies that components work together (service + real database, two modules, a message broker). "Narrow" integration tests one boundary; "broad" spins up many services. Testcontainers is a common tool.

notes.front: Contract test (consumer-driven contracts)?
notes.back: Consumer records its expectations of a provider's Application Programming Interface (API) as a contract; the provider verifies it in its own Continuous Integration (CI). Catches breaking changes between services without full End-to-End (E2E) environments. Tool: Pact.

notes.front: End-to-End (E2E) test?
notes.back: Exercises a full user journey through the deployed stack (browser/client → backend → database). Highest confidence per test, but slowest, flakiest and most expensive; keep few and focused on critical paths. Tools: Playwright, Cypress.

notes.front: System vs. acceptance testing?
notes.back: System: the whole integrated system against its requirements. Acceptance (incl. User Acceptance Testing (UAT)): does it satisfy business/user acceptance criteria; often owned by business stakeholders.

notes.front: Smoke vs. sanity test?
notes.back: Smoke: shallow, broad check that a build is basically alive ("does it start, does login work") before deeper testing. Sanity: narrow, quick check that a specific fix/area works after a change.

notes.front: Regression testing?
notes.back: Re-running tests to ensure changes didn't break existing behaviour. Every bug fix should add a regression test that reproduces the bug first.

notes.front: Load vs. stress vs. soak vs. spike testing?
notes.back:
• Load: expected peak traffic
  • Stress: beyond capacity, find the breaking point and failure mode
  • Soak/endurance: sustained load for hours/days (memory leaks, connection exhaustion)
  • Spike: sudden bursts
Tools: k6, Gatling, JMeter, Locust.

notes.front: Static vs. Dynamic Application Security Testing (SAST vs. DAST)?
notes.back: SAST: analyse source/bytecode without running it (Semgrep, CodeQL). DAST: attack the running application from outside (OWASP ZAP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project Zed Attack Proxy), Burp). Plus Software Composition Analysis (SCA) for vulnerable dependencies and penetration testing by humans.

notes.front: Fuzz testing?
notes.back: Feeding large volumes of random/mutated input to find crashes, hangs, memory errors and security bugs. Coverage-guided fuzzers (American Fuzzy Lop (AFL), libFuzzer, Go native fuzzing) evolve inputs that reach new code paths.

notes.front: Property-based testing?
notes.back: State a general property that must hold for all inputs; the framework generates many inputs and, on failure, shrinks to a minimal counterexample. Finds edge cases nobody thought of.

notes.front: Mutation testing?
notes.back: Tool injects small faults ("mutants": >→>=, +→-, remove a call) and reruns the suite. Killed mutant = some test failed. Surviving mutant = gap in assertions. Mutation score = killed / total. Tools: PIT (Java), Stryker (JS/C#), mutmut (Python), cargo-mutants (Rust).

notes.front: Exploratory testing?
notes.back: Unscripted, skilled testing where design and execution happen together, guided by a charter ("explore checkout with expired cards to discover pricing errors"), time-boxed, with notes. Finds the bugs scripted tests didn't imagine.

notes.front: Visual regression testing?
notes.back: Screenshot comparison of User Interface (UI) states against baselines to catch unintended layout/style changes. Needs stable rendering (fonts, animations, data) to avoid noise.

notes.front: Accessibility testing?
notes.back: Checking usability for people with disabilities against the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG): automated scanners (axe) catch roughly a third of issues; the rest need keyboard-only and screen-reader testing.

notes.front: Testing in production techniques?
notes.back: Canary releases, feature flags, dark launches/shadow traffic, A/B tests, synthetic monitoring, chaos experiments. Requires good observability and fast rollback.

notes.front: Alpha vs. beta testing?
notes.back: Alpha: internal users/testers in a controlled environment. Beta: real external users in real environments before general availability.

notes.front: The four Agile Testing Quadrants?
notes.back:
• Q1 technology-facing, supports team: unit, component
  • Q2 business-facing, supports team: functional, story/example tests, prototypes
  • Q3 business-facing, critiques product: exploratory, usability, User Acceptance Testing (UAT), alpha/beta
  • Q4 technology-facing, critiques product: performance, load, security, "-ilities"

notes.front: What is Behaviour-Driven Development (BDD) at its core?
notes.back: A collaboration practice: discover desired behaviour through conversations and concrete examples, formulate them as structured scenarios, then automate them as executable specifications / living documentation. The conversation is the primary value; automation is secondary.

notes.front: The three practices of BDD (Behaviour-Driven Development) per the Cucumber team?
notes.back: Discovery (collaborative conversations, e.g. Example Mapping) → Formulation (write examples as Gherkin scenarios) → Automation (step definitions make them executable).
notes.source: Cucumber / Seb Rose & Gáspár Nagy, The BDD Books

notes.front: Who are the "Three Amigos"?
notes.back: Business (product owner/analyst), development, and testing perspectives meeting before implementation to examine a story and agree on examples and acceptance criteria.

notes.front: What is Example Mapping and its card colours?
notes.back: Matt Wynne's (2015) time-boxed discovery technique: yellow = story, blue = rules (acceptance criteria), green = examples illustrating each rule, red = open questions. Many reds → not ready; many blues → story too big.

notes.front: What is Specification by Example?
notes.back: Gojko Adzic (2011): use concrete examples, refined collaboratively, as the single source of truth for requirements, tests and documentation ("living documentation").

notes.front: Gherkin keywords?
notes.back: Feature, Rule, Scenario (alias Example), Given, When, Then, And, But, Background, Scenario Outline (Scenario Template) + Examples, plus data tables, doc strings ("""), tags (@smoke) and comments (#).

notes.front: Role of Given / When / Then?
notes.back: Given = context/precondition (past state). When = the single event/action. Then = observable outcome. Rule of thumb: one When per scenario.

notes.front: Declarative vs. imperative Gherkin — which to prefer and why?
notes.back: Prefer declarative: describe what the user achieves ("When Sam logs in"), not how ("When I type sam into #user and click Submit"). UI details belong in step definitions, so scenarios survive UI changes and stay readable for business people.

notes.front: "One scenario, one behaviour" — why?
notes.back: Scenarios testing several rules are long, hard to name, fail for ambiguous reasons and hide which rule broke. Split by rule; use Scenario Outline only for genuinely tabular variations of one rule.

notes.front: Common Gherkin anti-patterns?
notes.back:
• Imperative, click-by-click steps
  • Scenarios as test scripts rather than documentation
  • Feature-length scenarios / multiple When
  • Scenarios depending on each other's state
  • Overused Scenario Outlines with huge tables
  • Vague scenarios with no concrete data
  • Incidental details (irrelevant IDs, timestamps) cluttering steps
  • Generic actors ("the user") instead of meaningful personas

notes.front: Why must scenarios be independent?
notes.back: Chained scenarios (B relies on data left by A) fail in cascades, can't run in parallel or in isolation, and make failures hard to diagnose. Each scenario sets up its own Given.

notes.front: What is the Background keyword for, and its pitfall?
notes.back: Shared Givens run before every scenario in a feature. Pitfall: long Backgrounds hide context the reader needs; keep it short and only for truly common setup.

notes.front: Does BDD (Behaviour-Driven Development) require Cucumber or end-to-end UI tests?
notes.back: No. Scenarios can be automated at any layer (domain, Application Programming Interface (API), UI). Many teams run most scenarios against the domain/API layer and only a few through the User Interface (UI). Plain unit-test frameworks with given/when/then naming also count.

notes.front: Scenario naming best practice?
notes.back: Name the behaviour/outcome and distinguish it from siblings: "Expired card is declined at checkout" rather than "Test checkout 3". The name list of a feature should read like a specification.

notes.front: How do BDD (Behaviour-Driven Development) and TDD (Test-Driven Development) relate?
notes.back: Double loop: an outer failing acceptance scenario (BDD) drives inner red-green-refactor unit cycles (TDD) until the scenario passes.

notes.front: Why are BDD (Behaviour-Driven Development) scenarios useful prompts for coding agents?
notes.back: They are concrete, executable acceptance criteria in natural language: the agent gets both the intent and a pass/fail check. Keep humans owning the scenarios; let the agent implement step definitions and code.

notes.front: Equivalence partitioning?
notes.back: Split input (and output) domains into classes the program should treat the same; test one representative per class, including invalid classes. E.g. age: <0, 0–17, 18–64, ≥65, non-numeric.

notes.front: Boundary Value Analysis (BVA)?
notes.back: Bugs cluster at partition edges (off-by-one, < vs <=). Test at, just below, and just above each boundary: for 18–64 test 17, 18, 19, 63, 64, 65.

notes.front: Decision table testing?
notes.back: Enumerate combinations of conditions and their expected actions in a table; each column becomes a test. Reveals missing or contradictory rules in business logic.

notes.front: State transition testing?
notes.back: Model the system as states + events. Test valid transitions, invalid transitions (e.g. ship a cancelled order), sequences, and loops. Draw the state diagram; missing arrows are often bugs.

notes.front: Pairwise (combinatorial) testing?
notes.back: Most interaction bugs involve 2 parameters, so cover every pair of values rather than every combination. Tools (PICT, AllPairs) shrink e.g. 3^10 = 59,049 combos to ~15–20 tests.

notes.front: Error guessing?
notes.back: Experience-based technique: use known fault patterns (null, empty, duplicates, concurrency, encoding) and past bugs to predict where defects hide. Keep a team checklist of past escapes.

notes.front: ZOMBIES heuristic (James Grenning)?
notes.back: Order for test-driving: Zero, One, Many (or More complex), Boundary behaviours, Interface definition, Exceptional behaviour, Simple scenarios / simple solutions.

notes.front: CORRECT boundary checklist (Hunt & Thomas)?
notes.back: Conformance (format), Ordering, Range, Reference (external dependencies/preconditions), Existence (null/empty/missing), Cardinality (0, 1, many), Time (ordering, timeouts, time zones).

notes.front: Right-BICEP?
notes.back: Are the results Right? Boundary conditions, Inverse relationships, Cross-check with other means, Error conditions forced, Performance within bounds.

notes.front: Classic data edge cases for strings?
notes.back: Empty, whitespace-only, very long, Unicode (emoji, combining characters, right-to-left text, zero-width chars), normalization (é as one vs two code points), case folding (Turkish İ), injection characters (' " < ; --), null bytes.

notes.front: Classic numeric edge cases?
notes.back: 0, -1, 1, min/max integer and overflow, NaN, ±Infinity, -0.0, floating-point rounding (0.1+0.2), money in floats (use decimals/minor units), division by zero, very large/small magnitudes.

notes.front: Classic date/time edge cases?
notes.back: Daylight Saving Time (DST) gaps/overlaps, time zones and Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) offsets with half hours, leap years (Feb 29, year 2100 isn't one), leap seconds, month-end arithmetic (Jan 31 + 1 month), epoch/2038 overflow, clock skew, locales. Inject a clock; never call "now" directly.

notes.front: Classic collection edge cases?
notes.back: Empty, one element, duplicates, already sorted / reverse sorted, very large, contains nulls, mutation during iteration, pagination boundaries (exactly page size, page size + 1).

notes.front: Distributed-systems edge cases?
notes.back: Timeouts, retries and idempotency (duplicate delivery), out-of-order messages, partial failure, network partitions, slow (not dead) dependencies, concurrent updates/race conditions, clock skew, cache staleness.

notes.front: Security-flavoured edge cases?
notes.back: Authorization boundaries (access another tenant's ID — Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR)), unauthenticated calls, expired/forged tokens, oversized payloads, path traversal (../), injection, rate limits, privilege changes mid-session.

notes.front: Property-based testing: common property patterns?
notes.back:
• Round-trip: decode(encode(x)) == x
  • Invariants: sort keeps length and elements
  • Idempotence: f(f(x)) == f(x)
  • Oracle/differential: compare to a simple reference implementation
  • Commutativity / "different paths, same destination"
  • Hard to compute, easy to verify
notes.source: Scott Wlaschin, "Choosing properties for property-based testing"

notes.front: What is metamorphic testing?
notes.back: When there's no oracle, check relations between outputs of related inputs. E.g. search results for "A AND B" ⊆ results for "A"; rotating an image shouldn't change a classifier's label. Introduced by T.Y. Chen et al. (1998).

notes.front: What is shrinking and why does it matter?
notes.back: After a property-based test finds a failing input, the framework simplifies it to a minimal reproducing case (e.g. [0, -1] instead of a 300-element list), making the root cause obvious.

notes.front: How do you systematically find edge cases in an unfamiliar function?
notes.back:
1. List inputs, outputs, state and dependencies
  2. Partition each and mark boundaries
  3. Walk ZOMBIES/CORRECT checklists
  4. Model states and invalid transitions
  5. Ask "what can the environment do?" (time, failure, concurrency)
  6. Add property-based tests to find what you missed
  7. Run mutation testing to see which branches have weak assertions

notes.front: How can past production incidents improve edge-case detection?
notes.back: Defects cluster: mine incident/bug history for recurring categories, turn each escape into a regression test, and add the pattern to the team's error-guessing checklist.

notes.front: Characteristics of a good test name?
notes.back: States the scenario and expected outcome ("returns_empty_list_when_no_orders"). When it fails, the name alone should tell you what behaviour broke.

notes.front: Why one logical assertion (behaviour) per test?
notes.back: Failures pinpoint one behaviour; tests stay short and readable. Several asserts on one outcome object are fine; testing several behaviours is not.

notes.front: DAMP vs. DRY in tests?
notes.back: Production code favours Don't Repeat Yourself (DRY); tests favour Descriptive And Meaningful Phrases (DAMP): some duplication is fine if each test reads standalone. Extract helpers/builders for noise, not for logic.

notes.front: Why avoid logic (loops, conditionals) in tests?
notes.back: Logic in tests can contain bugs and often mirrors the implementation, so both share the same mistake. Prefer literal expected values or parameterized cases.

notes.front: What is a tautological test?
notes.back: A test whose expected value is computed the same way as the code (or asserts what a mock was told to return). It can never fail for a real bug. Very common in Artificial Intelligence (AI)-generated tests.

notes.front: Test data builders / object mothers?
notes.back: Factories with sensible defaults so each test sets only the fields relevant to it (anOrder().withExpiredCard().build()). Keeps incidental detail out of tests.

notes.front: Every bug fix should start with…?
notes.back: A failing test that reproduces the bug. It proves you understood it, verifies the fix, and prevents regression.

notes.front: How to make time and randomness testable?
notes.back: Inject a clock and a seeded random source instead of calling global now()/random(). Log seeds on failure so runs are reproducible.

notes.front: How to keep a test suite fast?
notes.back: Push most tests to small/unit level, use fakes for slow dependencies, parallelize, avoid sleeps (poll with timeouts), share expensive fixtures carefully, run slow suites (mutation, soak, full E2E (End-to-End)) nightly rather than per commit.

notes.front: Where should mutation testing run in a pipeline?
notes.back: Usually nightly or post-merge, or incrementally on changed code only; full mutation runs are too slow for every merge request.
notes.source: agentpatterns.ai, "Mutation Testing as a Quality Gate"

notes.front: What does a healthy test portfolio look like?
notes.back: Fast, deterministic tests at the bottom giving quick feedback; a solid integration layer; few critical-path E2E (End-to-End) tests; contract tests between services; exploratory and production monitoring on top. Shape (pyramid vs. trophy) depends on architecture.

notes.front: Single most important practice when working with coding agents (per Anthropic's Claude Code guidance)?
notes.back: Give the agent a way to verify its own work: a check that returns pass/fail (tests, build exit code, linter, fixture diff, screenshot comparison). Without it, "looks done" is the only stopping signal and you become the verification loop.

notes.front: What does "use red/green TDD" mean as a prompt to an agent?
notes.back: Shorthand for: write the tests first, run them and confirm they fail, then implement until they pass. Models understand the phrase; it guards against non-working code and unnecessary code.
notes.source: Simon Willison, Agentic Engineering Patterns: "Red/green TDD"

notes.front: Why is the "confirm it fails first" step especially important with agents?
notes.back: Agents readily write tests that already pass (wrong target, weak assertion), giving a false green that never exercised the new code.

notes.front: How should you prompt an agent to fix a bug?
notes.back: Describe the symptom, likely location, and what "fixed" means; ask it to write a failing test that reproduces the issue, then fix the root cause (not suppress the error), then show the passing output.

notes.front: Ways to gate an agent's "done" on a check, from soft to hard?
notes.back:
• In the prompt: "run the tests and iterate"
  • Session goal re-checked by a separate evaluator
  • Deterministic hook (e.g. a Stop hook) that blocks finishing until the script passes
  • A second model (verification subagent) that tries to refute the result

notes.front: Why are hooks better than instructions for enforcing test discipline?
notes.back: Instructions in CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md are advisory and can be ignored or lost in long context; hooks run deterministically every time (e.g. run tests after each edit, block writes to protected test folders).

notes.front: Why should a different agent/session review or test the implementation?
notes.back: A fresh context sees only the diff and criteria, not the reasoning that produced it, so it is less biased toward the code it would have written. Patterns: Writer/Reviewer sessions; one instance writes tests, another writes code.

notes.front: Key rule to prevent agents gaming the tests?
notes.back: Don't let the same agent instance modify both the tests and the code under test in the same task. Treat human-approved tests as the specification; agents may propose test changes, but a human approves them.
notes.source: LessWrong/GreaterWrong comment on reward hacking; Medium, "Test-Driven Agentic Development"

notes.front: Typical ways agents "reward hack" a test suite?
notes.back: Deleting or skipping failing tests, weakening assertions, special-casing test inputs, hardcoding expected outputs, catching and swallowing exceptions, mocking away the thing under test, or editing fixtures to match buggy output. Review test diffs as carefully as code diffs.

notes.front: Why is coverage especially misleading for AI (Artificial Intelligence)-generated tests?
notes.back: Agents can produce high-coverage, all-green suites quickly whose assertions catch nothing. Coverage proves a line ran; mutation testing proves the suite would notice a regression.

notes.front: Rule of thumb: "no generated test enters the suite without…"
notes.back: …proving it can fail. Verify by mutating the code under test (manually or with a mutation tool) and checking the test goes red.
notes.source: web-developpeur.com, "Your AI Writes Tests That Can Never Fail"

notes.front: What is the "test homogenization trap"?
notes.back: Tests generated by the same model that wrote the code share its blind spots and misunderstandings, so the suite confirms rather than challenges the implementation. Mitigate with human-written examples, property-based tests, mutation testing and independent reviewers.

notes.front: How can mutation testing be made adversarial with agents?
notes.back: One agent generates mutants targeting blind spots; another writes tests to kill them, iterating on mutation score (e.g. the AdverTest framework).

notes.front: What is "agentic manual testing"?
notes.back: Having the agent exercise the code like a human would (e.g. python -c "...", a throwaway demo in /tmp, curl against a dev server, browser automation). Often reveals issues the automated tests missed; then fix via red/green TDD.

notes.front: Why ask agents for evidence rather than claims of success?
notes.back: "Tests pass" is an assertion; the command, its output, or a screenshot is evidence. Reviewing evidence is faster than re-running verification and works for unattended sessions.

notes.front: How should test specs be prepared before a large agentic task?
notes.back: Explore → plan → implement. For big features, have the agent interview you about edge cases and trade-offs, write a self-contained SPEC.md naming files, interfaces, out-of-scope items, and an end-to-end verification step; implement in a fresh session.

notes.front: Tests as prompts: how does a test act as a specification for an agent?
notes.back: A test name like it('returns only valid emails from a mixed list') plus examples is a precise, checkable spec. Small, one-behaviour-at-a-time tests keep the model on narrow goals rather than bloated implementations.
notes.source: Tweag Agentic Coding Handbook, TDD workflow

notes.front: Danger of adversarial review subagents?
notes.back: Asked to find gaps, a reviewer will usually report some even when work is sound; chasing all of them leads to over-engineering and tests for impossible cases. Restrict findings to correctness and stated requirements.

notes.front: What test-related content belongs in CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md?
notes.back: How to run tests (exact commands, single-test invocation), preferred runners, test-first rule, what "done" means, conventions (avoid mocks here, use fixtures there). Keep it short; enforce must-always rules with hooks instead.

notes.front: Why write characterization tests before letting an agent refactor legacy code?
notes.back: They lock in current behaviour so the agent's refactor can be verified mechanically; otherwise behaviour changes go unnoticed because there's no oracle.

notes.front: What are FAIL_TO_PASS and PASS_TO_PASS tests (SWE-bench)?
notes.back: Software Engineering benchmark (SWE-bench) verifies an agent's patch with tests that failed before and must pass after (the fix works) and tests that passed before and must still pass (no regressions). A good mental model for any agent task.

notes.front: How do you test features that call a Large Language Model (LLM)?
notes.back: Evals: curated datasets of inputs with expected properties; deterministic checks (schema, contains/not-contains, tool called) where possible; model-graded rubrics ("LLM-as-a-judge") calibrated against human labels; run repeatedly because outputs are non-deterministic; track scores across prompt/model changes like a regression suite.

notes.front: pass@k vs. pass^k?
notes.back: pass@k: at least one of k attempts succeeds (capability). pass^k: all k attempts succeed (reliability/consistency), from τ-bench (2024). Agents in production need pass^k.

notes.front: How can you make an agent's test suite more trustworthy than "green"?
notes.back: Combine: human-owned acceptance scenarios, red-first verification, property-based tests, mutation score gates, protected test files, separate writer/reviewer agents, and evidence (logs/screenshots) in the Pull Request (PR).

notes.front: Does AI-assisted development reduce the need for testing discipline?
notes.back: No — it amplifies existing practices. Strong test feedback lets agents iterate autonomously; weak suites let them generate plausible but wrong code faster. The Google DevOps Research and Assessment (DORA) 2025 report frames AI as an amplifier of existing engineering practices.
notes.source: DORA 2025 State of AI-assisted Software Development

notes.front: Plan-first workflow and TDD (Test-Driven Development) with agents?
notes.back: Have the agent produce a plan, including what the failing tests will be, before touching code. Agreeing on "what red looks like" up front captures most of TDD's value before any line is written.

notes.front: What is a verification subagent?
notes.back: A separate model instance with its own context and limited tools whose only job is to check (and try to refute) the main agent's result against criteria, so the worker isn't grading itself.
